verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, in keeping with the promise of life that is in Christ Jesus,
to Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
I am grateful to God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as my ancestors did, as I constantly remember you in my prayers, night and day,
verse.note: The phrase stands between two clauses and can attach to either: Paul remembers Timothy in his prayers night and day, or he longs night and day to see him. The English keeps the phrase at the same point, so both readings stay open.

verse.text: longing to see you, remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy.
I have been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, a faith that lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and, I am convinced, lives in you as well.
For this reason I remind you to rekindle the gift of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands;
for God did not give us a spirit of cowardice, but of power and love and self-discipline.
verse.note: The traditional 'spirit of fear' suggests fear in general, and 'timidity' suggests shyness. In Greek usage this word is the regular term for cowardice, the failure of nerve that makes someone shrink from danger or duty. It is distinct from the ordinary word for fear, which can be a good thing. The charge not to be ashamed in the next verse fits this stronger sense.

Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so this may be a disposition God gives ('a spirit of power') or the Holy Spirit himself ('the Spirit, who produces power'). Most translations print a lower-case 'spirit', and that is followed here. Many interpreters think the Holy Spirit, named in verse 14, is in view.

The word occurs only here in the New Testament. It belongs to a family of words for sober good sense and moderation, and it can mean either the exercise of self-control or sound, level-headed judgment. Older versions have 'a sound mind'; most modern ones have 'self-control' or 'self-discipline'.

verse.text: So do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, or of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the good news, by the power of God.
verse.note: 'Gospel' has become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for the public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

verse.text: He saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace. This grace was given to us in Christ Jesus before the long ages began,

note.traditional: before the world began; before times eternal; before the ages began

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'before age-long times', the adjective usually translated 'eternal' joined to the plural 'times'. 'Before eternal times' makes little sense in English, so the phrase is rendered as the long ages of the world's history, with God's grace given before they began. The same expression occurs in Romans 16:25 and Titus 1:2.

verse.text: but has now been revealed through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the good news.
verse.note: In the wider Greek world this word was used for the visible manifestation of a god coming to help, and for the arrival or accession of a ruler. 'Savior' was likewise a title given to gods and emperors. A first-century reader would have heard both words as claiming for Jesus honours that others claimed for themselves. Elsewhere in these letters the word usually refers to Christ's future coming; here it refers to his first.

verse.text: For this good news I was appointed herald and apostle and teacher.
verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'teacher of the Gentiles', and older English versions follow them. The shorter reading is printed in the SBLGNT. The longer one is widely regarded as an addition drawn from the parallel in 1 Timothy 2:7.

verse.text: For this reason I also suffer these things. But I am not ashamed, for I know the one I have trusted, and I am convinced that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him until that day.

note.term: what I have entrusted to him
note.traditional: that which I have committed unto him

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'my deposit', a legal term for property left in someone's safekeeping. It can mean what Paul has entrusted to God (his life, his work, his future) or what God has entrusted to Paul (the message, as in verse 14, where Timothy is to guard 'the good deposit'). Most translations take it the first way, as here. A substantial number of scholars prefer the second because of verse 14.

verse.text: Hold to the pattern of sound words that you heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
Guard the good thing entrusted to you, through the Holy Spirit who lives in us.
You know this, that everyone in Asia has turned away from me, among them Phygelus and Hermogenes.
verse.note: This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of modern Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city. It is not the continent. 'Everyone' is probably a broad statement of general desertion rather than a literal count. Nothing further is known of Phygelus and Hermogenes.

verse.text: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain;
verse.note: Paul prays for Onesiphorus's household now and for Onesiphorus himself 'on that day', and he greets only the household in 4:19. Many interpreters conclude that Onesiphorus had died. Others think he was simply away from home. The text does not say, and the question bears on later debates about prayer for the dead.

verse.text: on the contrary, when he came to Rome he searched hard for me and found me—
may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day—and how much service he gave in Ephesus, you know very well.

note.term: may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord

verse.note: 'Lord' occurs twice, and it is unclear whether both refer to the same person. One common reading takes the first as Christ and the second as God the Father, the judge on the last day. Others take the doubling as a fixed form of prayer. The Greek also plays on 'found' in verse 17: Onesiphorus found Paul, and Paul prays that he may find mercy.

verse.text: You then, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus,
and what you heard from me before many witnesses, entrust to faithful people who will be competent to teach others as well.

note.traditional: in the presence of many witnesses / among many witnesses

verse.note: The Greek is literally "through many witnesses." Most translators take it as an idiom for "with many witnesses present," perhaps recalling a public occasion such as Timothy's commissioning. It could instead mean that the teaching was confirmed by, or passed on through, many witnesses.

verse.text: Take your share of hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No one serving as a soldier gets entangled in the business of everyday life; his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.
Likewise, if anyone competes as an athlete, he is not crowned unless he competes by the rules.
The farmer who does the hard work ought to be the first to share in the crops.
Think over what I am saying, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.
Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, of the seed of David, according to my good news,
verse.note: "Gospel" has become a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for the announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between the two renderings.

verse.text: for which I suffer hardship, even to the point of chains, like a criminal. But the word of God is not chained.
For this reason I endure everything for the sake of the chosen, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory.
The saying is trustworthy: For if we died with him, we will also live with him;
verse.note: This translation normally renders this adjective "faithful," as in verses 2 and 13. Applied to a saying, "faithful" is unnatural in modern English, so "trustworthy" is used, as in most recent translations. The formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and Titus. The lines that follow, through verse 13, are widely thought to quote an early hymn or confession.

verse.text: if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he too will deny us;
if we are faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself.
verse.note: The verb can mean "fail to believe" or "prove unfaithful." The play on "he remains faithful" favours the second, and the rendering keeps that echo. It is also debated whether this line is a comfort (his faithfulness outlasts our failure) or a warning (he stays true to his word, including the warning of verse 12).

verse.text: Keep reminding people of these things, solemnly charging them before the Lord not to fight over words, which is useful for nothing and ruins those who listen.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided here between "before the Lord" and "before God." The SBLGNT text translated here reads "the Lord"; other critical editions and translations based on them read "God." The sense is hardly affected.

verse.text: Make every effort to present yourself to God as one who has passed the test, a worker with no cause for shame, guiding the word of truth along a straight path.

note.term: guiding the word of truth along a straight path
note.traditional: rightly dividing the word of truth / rightly handling the word of truth

verse.note: The verb is rare. Its only earlier known uses are in the Greek version of Proverbs (3:6; 11:5), where it means to cut or make a road straight. The rendering follows that usage: the message is to be kept on a straight course, in contrast to the teachers of verses 16–18 who have strayed. Most modern translations paraphrase as "correctly handling"; the older "rightly dividing" rests on the word's parts, not on its attested use.

verse.text: But keep away from profane, empty talk, for those who engage in it will advance further into ungodliness,
and their word will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus,
who have strayed from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they are overturning the faith of some.

note.term: the resurrection has already taken place

verse.note: These teachers apparently held that resurrection was a purely spiritual event already experienced by believers, perhaps at conversion or baptism, leaving no future bodily resurrection to hope for. The details of their teaching are not known. Paul treats it as striking at the centre of the faith (compare 1 Corinthians 15).

verse.text: Nevertheless, God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord turn away from wrongdoing.”
verse.note: A seal was an inscription or stamp marking ownership and authenticity. The first inscription quotes Numbers 16:5 in its Greek form, from the story of Korah's rebellion against Moses. The second is not an exact quotation of any one passage but echoes scriptural language, possibly including the same story (Numbers 16:26) and Isaiah 26:13.

verse.text: Now in a large house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use and some for dishonorable.
So if anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honorable use, made holy, useful to the master, prepared for every good work.

note.traditional: from these / from what is dishonorable

verse.note: "These" most naturally refers to the dishonorable vessels of verse 20, that is, the false teachers and their influence. It could also refer more loosely to the errors and wrongdoing just described. Some translations make the second reading explicit.

verse.text: Flee the desires of youth, and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
Have nothing to do with foolish and uninstructed disputes, knowing that they breed fights.
And a slave of the Lord must not fight, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, patient when wronged,
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a slave, someone owned by a master, not a hired servant. "Servant" is traditional and softens this. The phrase also echoes the Old Testament title "servant of the Lord," given to Moses, David and the prophets, which the Greek Scriptures often render with this word; there it is a title of honour as well as of ownership.

verse.text: instructing opponents with gentleness, in the hope that God may grant them a turning back that leads to knowledge of the truth,
verse.note: "Meekness" now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek does not. The word describes a gentle, unassertive manner. "Gentleness" is the usual rendering in modern translations.

"Repentance" now centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets' call to "return" to God, describes a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep "repentance" as an established term understood to include a change of life.

verse.text: and that they may come to their senses and escape the devil’s snare, having been captured alive by him to do his will.

note.term: by him to do his will
note.traditional: taken captive by him at his will / captured by him to do his will

verse.note: The Greek uses two different pronouns, and it is disputed whom each refers to. The rendering follows the majority view that both refer to the devil. Alternatively, the opponents escape the devil who captured them in order to do God's will, or they are "captured alive" by the Lord's slave to do God's will.

verse.text: But know this: in the last days hard times will set in.
For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy,
heartless, implacable, slanderous, without self-control, savage, with no love for what is good,
treacherous, reckless, puffed up with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,
holding to an outward form of godliness but having denied its power. Avoid these people as well.
For among them are those who worm their way into households and take captive weak-willed women who are loaded down with sins and led by all kinds of desires,
verse.note: The Greek is a diminutive of 'woman' used with contempt, literally 'little women'. It describes the particular women these teachers targeted, not women in general. English versions vary between 'silly', 'weak', 'gullible' and 'weak-willed'; the following phrases about sins and desires suggest that moral weakness is meant, not lack of intelligence.

verse.text: always learning and never able to arrive at knowledge of the truth.
Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth: people whose minds are corrupted, who have failed the test where the faith is concerned.
verse.note: These names do not appear in the Old Testament. Jewish tradition gave them to the Egyptian magicians who matched Moses' signs before Pharaoh (Exodus 7–9) until their powers failed and they were exposed. The author assumes his reader knows the story.

The word describes something that has been tested and found not genuine, as with coinage or metal that does not pass assay. 'Reprobate' now suggests general depravity, which the Greek does not say. Most modern versions use 'disqualified' or 'rejected', which express the same idea.

verse.text: But they will make no further progress, for their folly will be plain to everyone, as the folly of those two also came to be.
But you have followed closely my teaching, my way of life, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my endurance,
verse.note: In a list of personal qualities alongside patience and endurance, the word could equally mean 'faithfulness', that is, Paul's reliability. Most translations keep 'faith', and the Greek does not settle the question.

verse.text: my persecutions, my sufferings, the kind that happened to me in Antioch, in Iconium, in Lystra, the kind of persecutions I endured. And from all of them the Lord rescued me.

note.term: in Antioch, in Iconium, in Lystra

verse.note: These are three cities in the south of Asia Minor where, according to Acts 13–14, Paul was driven out, threatened with stoning, and finally stoned and left for dead. Acts 16:1 places Timothy at Lystra, so these are events he would have known about from his own home region. The Antioch meant is Pisidian Antioch, not Antioch in Syria.

verse.text: Indeed, all who want to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted,
while evil people and charlatans will progress from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.
verse.note: The word originally meant a sorcerer or enchanter, and by this period was commonly used for a swindler or fraud. Most translations choose 'impostors'. 'Charlatans' is used here because it keeps the suggestion of bogus powers, which fits the comparison with Pharaoh's magicians in verse 8; whether actual magical practice is alleged is uncertain.

verse.text: But as for you, remain in what you have learned and become convinced of, knowing from whom you learned it,

note.traditional: of whom thou hast learned them

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have a plural here, meaning 'from which people', which probably takes in Timothy's mother and grandmother (1:5) as well as Paul. Many later manuscripts have the singular, pointing to Paul alone. English cannot show the difference without paraphrase.

verse.text: and that from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
Every scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness,

note.traditional: All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable

verse.note: The Greek has no verb 'is' and no article, so two questions arise. The phrase can mean 'every scripture', passage by passage, or 'all Scripture' as a whole; and the sentence can be read 'every scripture is God-breathed and useful' or 'every God-breathed scripture is also useful'. Most translations and scholars take the first construction, as here, and many prefer 'all Scripture'; the practical difference is small, since the writings in view are the sacred writings of verse 15.

note.traditional: inspired by God; given by inspiration of God

verse.note: This rare compound joins 'God' and 'breathe' and occurs only here in the New Testament. 'Inspired' comes from the Latin translation and in modern English suggests artistic brilliance, whereas the Greek says that the writings come from God's breath. Several modern versions render it 'God-breathed' or 'breathed out by God'; the word states the origin of scripture without explaining how this happened.

verse.text: so that the person who belongs to God may be complete, completely equipped for every good work.

note.term: the person who belongs to God

verse.note: The Greek word is the general one for a human being, not the word for a male. 'Man of God' is also a title in the Greek Old Testament for figures such as Moses and Elijah, and it is applied to Timothy in 1 Timothy 6:11. Many scholars therefore think the phrase here refers especially to Timothy as a Christian leader, while others take it of any believer; the rendering leaves both open.

The Greek uses two words from the same root, an adjective meaning fit or complete and a verb meaning to fit out fully. The repetition in English reproduces this echo. The adjective describes being fully suited to a task, not moral perfection.

verse.text: I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus, who is going to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom:

note.term: by his appearing and his kingdom
note.traditional: at his appearing and his kingdom

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have a bare accusative, the Greek construction for the thing one swears by, so Paul is invoking Christ's appearing and reign as part of the oath. Later manuscripts read ‘at his appearing’, attaching the phrase to the judging, and the King James Version follows them. ‘Appearing’ translates a word used for the visible manifestation of a god or the arrival of a ruler.

verse.text: proclaim the word; be on hand, whether the time is right or not; reprove, rebuke, encourage, with all patience and instruction.
verse.note: The verb means to stand by or be at one's post, and can also carry the sense of pressing on with something, so some translations have ‘be persistent’ or ‘be urgent’. The same verb returns in verse 6, where the time of Paul's departure ‘is at hand’; the rendering here keeps that echo.

verse.text: For a time will come when people will not put up with sound teaching, but following their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, because their ears itch,
and they will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths.
But you, keep a clear head in everything, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, carry out your service in full.
verse.note: The Greek word meant service rendered or a task carried out on someone's behalf. ‘Ministry’ is the traditional rendering and remains common, but it now suggests a clerical profession, which the word did not. It recurs in verse 11, where it may refer either to personal help for Paul or to the work of the mission.

verse.text: For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand.

note.term: poured out as a drink offering
note.traditional: ready to be offered / poured out as a drink offering

verse.note: Wine was poured out alongside a sacrifice in both Jewish and Greco-Roman worship, and Paul pictures his approaching death as such an offering, as he also does in Philippians 2:17. ‘Departure’ in the same verse was a common euphemism for death; the word was also used of a ship casting off or an army breaking camp.

verse.text: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
verse.note: The Greek phrase was an established expression for keeping one's pledge or staying loyal, so the sense may be ‘I have kept faith’, that is, remained true to the commission. The other reading is that Paul has guarded the faith as a body of belief entrusted to him, in line with the charge to guard the deposit earlier in the letter. The traditional wording allows both.

verse.text: As for what remains, the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day, and not only me but also all who have loved his appearing.
verse.note: The word is the victor's wreath awarded at athletic games, not a king's crown, and it continues the picture of the contest and the race in verse 7, with the Lord as the judge who awards the prize. ‘Of righteousness’ may mean the wreath given for a righteous life or the wreath that consists in being declared righteous; interpreters are divided.

verse.text: Do your best to come to me soon,
for Demas has deserted me, because he loved the present age, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia.
verse.note: Some important early manuscripts read ‘Gaul’ instead. Even with the reading ‘Galatia’ the reference is uncertain, since Greek writers of the period could use that name for Gaul as well as for the region in Asia Minor. Most translations print ‘Galatia’.

verse.text: Luke alone is with me. Pick up Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service,
and I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus.
When you come, bring the cloak that I left in Troas with Carpus, and the scrolls, especially the parchments.
verse.note: Books at this time were normally papyrus rolls, so ‘scrolls’ gives a truer picture than ‘books’. ‘Parchments’ is a Latin loanword for prepared animal skin, possibly parchment notebooks; what they contained (Scripture, Paul's own notes, personal documents) is unknown. A minority view takes ‘especially’ as ‘that is’, making the scrolls and the parchments the same items.

verse.text: Alexander the metalworker did me a great deal of harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds.
verse.note: The word originally named a worker in copper or bronze but by this period was used for a smith or metalworker of any kind. ‘Coppersmith’ is the traditional rendering and may be right, but it is more specific than the Greek requires.

note.traditional: the Lord reward him according to his works

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have a future tense, a statement that the Lord will deal with Alexander; later manuscripts have a wish, ‘may the Lord repay him’, which the King James Version follows. The wording echoes Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12. The same verb is used in verse 8 for the Lord awarding the crown.

verse.text: You too must be on your guard against him, for he strongly opposed our words.
At my first defence no one came to my side; everyone deserted me. May it not be counted against them.
verse.note: The word is the legal term for a defendant's speech in court. Most scholars take this to be the preliminary hearing of Paul's current trial; an older view refers it to an earlier trial that ended in release. ‘Came to my side’ uses a verb for appearing in court in someone's support.

verse.text: But the Lord stood by my side and gave me strength, so that through me the proclamation might be carried out in full and all the Gentiles might hear it; and I was rescued from the lion's mouth.
verse.note: Greek has one word for ‘nations’ and ‘Gentiles’ (non-Jewish peoples), and the phrase could equally be rendered ‘all the nations’. ‘Gentiles’ is chosen here because Paul is speaking of his own commission as apostle to the non-Jewish world, and most translations do the same.

The phrase echoes Psalm 22:21 and the story of Daniel, and most interpreters take it as a figure for extreme danger, not a literal sentence to the arena. Suggestions that the lion is the emperor, or Satan, go back to early readers but cannot be confirmed.

verse.text: The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus.
Erastus stayed in Corinth, and Trophimus I left in Miletus, ill.
Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus greets you, and so do Pudens, Linus, Claudia and all the brothers and sisters.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to refer to a mixed group of men and women, here the fellow believers with Paul, among whom a woman, Claudia, has just been named. ‘Brothers’ alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are meant. Many recent translations render it the same way.

verse.text: The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all.
verse.note: In the first sentence ‘your’ is singular, addressed to Timothy; in the second ‘you’ is plural. The closing blessing therefore reaches beyond Timothy to the community with him, which suggests the letter was expected to be heard by others.
